paras: The Chattanooga jail mob of September 1882 was a gathering of a crowd reported at 5,000 around the jail at Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the night of September 18, 1882, demanding the Taylor brothers, who were wanted for killing the Hamilton County sheriff and his deputy. The brothers had not in fact been captured, and after a committee from the crowd searched the jail and found them absent, the crowd dispersed without harming anyone. Wire reports noted that leading citizens took part, and dispatches the next day labeled the crowd "Disappointed Lynchers."

On September 14, Sheriff W. T. Cate of Hamilton County and Deputy Sheriff John J. Conway were taking three prisoners by train from Chattanooga to the state Supreme Court at Knoxville, among them John Taylor, under a ten-year sentence for killing Captain John Fletcher. According to the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, Taylor's brothers Bob and Andy boarded at Sweetwater, shot Conway dead and mortally wounded Cate, freed John, and forced the crew to run the train to Lenoir's, where the three escaped. The Chronicle identified the co-prisoners J. L. Carter as "white" and Ed Bivens as "colored" and referred to Carter as "the other white prisoner," giving no separate race for Taylor.
By September 18 the country was being searched for the brothers, though nothing had been heard of them since the Thursday night after the killings.

About dark on September 18, according to a Nashville American dispatch, word spread in Chattanooga that the killers had been captured and would arrive by train at 10:30 p.m., and a large crowd gathered at the depot. A second report then held that the train had stopped on the outskirts and the prisoners had been taken secretly to the jail; the fire bells were rung and, in the American's words, "the whole populace was on the streets." A wire dispatch filed at 11:15 p.m. put the crowd about the jail at five thousand people "demanding the prisoners."

The wire accounts said a committee of five "was permitted to examine the jail" and reported that the Taylors were not there, while the Nashville American said that at 11:30 p.m. "a mob broke into the jail" and the committee searched every cell. Excitement was described as intense, and the crowd slowly left the jail toward midnight.

That night Governor Hawkins raised his reward for the brothers from $5,000 to $15,000, bringing the total offered to $16,500. No report of arrests or any official inquiry into the crowd at the jail appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers mainly through two short wire dispatches, one filed the night of September 18 and printed the next morning in Savannah, Portland and Wheeling, and a follow-up of September 19 carried in Richmond, Savannah, Dallas and Knoxville. Headlines ranged from "A Mob About the Chattanooga Jail" in the Savannah Morning News to "Disappointed Lynchers" in the Richmond Dispatch and "A Disappointed Mob" in the Dallas Daily Herald. The night dispatch remarked that "the best citizens of Chattanooga figured conspicuously in the mob," without further comment.

A condensed version reached weeklies such as the Bolivar Bulletin late in September. The Rugbeian, a weekly in Morgan County, Tennessee, printed the Nashville American's account and an editorial that found Chattanooga's excitement unsurprising after the murder of "two prominent and esteemed citizens" but called the jail scene "a wild, unreasoning, mad display of indignation, very inconsistent in a civilized community." The editorial attributed the tendency "to lynch criminals" to "legal and disciplinary laxities" rather than revenge, concluding that "the populace is more law-abiding than the law." None of the reports describes the Taylors or the crowd by race.

Accounts differ on how the committee entered the jail: the wire reports said it was permitted in, while the Nashville American said the mob broke in. The reward was given as $6,500 in the Savannah Morning News but as $16,500 in other papers, which the Nashville American explained by the governor's increase.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd surrounded the Chattanooga jail at night demanding men it believed held there for killing the sheriff and his deputy, and a Sept. 19 dispatch called them 'Disappointed Lynchers'; no one was found or harmed, and no paper describes the wanted men as Black (A2, A3, A6, A13, A1).
A crowd reported at 5,000 demanded the prisoners in order to punish them for the killings of Sheriff Cate and Deputy Conway, but the men were not in the jail and no one was killed (A3, A6, A13).
The Associated-style wire dispatches and a separate Nashville American dispatch agree on the rumor, the crowd at the jail, the committee of five and the dispersal (A3, A6, A13).

accounts.label: Wire follow-up, Sept. 19
accounts.gist: A committee of five from the crowd surrounding the jail was permitted to examine it, reported the men were not there, and the crowd dispersed.

accounts.label: Nashville American dispatch
accounts.gist: The rumor began about dark; a crowd met the expected train at the depot, then heard the prisoners had been secretly taken to the jail; fire bells rang, and at 11:30 p.m. 'a mob broke into the jail' and a committee of five searched every cell.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the short dispatches under heads such as 'The Taylor Brothers. A Mob About the Chattanooga Jail', 'Disappointed Lynchers' and 'Were Not There' without comment.

The Rugbeian excused Chattanooga's 'intense excitement' over two 'prominent and esteemed citizens' murdered, yet called the jail display 'very inconsistent in a civilized community' and blamed lynching on 'legal and disciplinary laxities'.

conflicts.note: The wire dispatches say the committee was 'permitted'; only the Nashville American says the mob broke in. Neither source is clearly better.
The Savannah figure is likely a dropped digit; the Nashville American explains $16,500 as the governor's raised $15,000 plus other offers.

record_check.dossier: No one harmed; targets sought were Bob, Andy and John Taylor, who were not in the jail
Not stated; the Knoxville Chronicle's phrase 'the other white prisoner' for a co-prisoner implies John Taylor was white
Killing Sheriff W. T. Cate and Deputy John J. Conway on Sept. 14
The Taylors were at large; the crowd only believed them jailed
At least 9 white papers opened, Sept. 19 to Sept. 28, plus further reprints into October
No paper describes the targets or crowd by race; the targets appear to have been white, so the episode is likely outside scope
